generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, marking criteria make the standard explicit for any piece of assessed work. They usually judge the depth of your knowledge and understanding, the clarity and structure of how you communicate it, and your critical evaluation rather than mere description. Reading your own draft against those dimensions, before you submit, is how you stop guessing what strong work looks like in any subject.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students applying the same marking criteria to their own work before submitting.

Student A reads the work through, feels it is fine, and submits. Asked which band it meets on critical evaluation, Student A cannot say: the work describes its material well but does not weigh it. Student A judged the work by effort and length, not against the criteria, and so missed that it sat a band lower than hoped.

Student B reads the work against each dimension in turn. Knowledge: strong. Communication: clear, though one section wanders. Critical evaluation: thin, mostly description. Student B can name the band each dimension meets and why, and revises the weakest part before submitting. The judgement is reasoned and tied to the criteria.

Both had the same criteria. Only Student B applied them, and turned the appraisal into stronger work.
generatedProse.summary: Marking criteria set out the standard your work is judged against, by dimension and level. Applying them to your own draft is self-assessment: you read as a marker would, name the band each dimension meets, and revise where it falls short. You can now appraise a piece of work against criteria and justify the judgement. The next lesson does the same for the feedback you receive.

check.body: What lets a student justify the grade a piece of their own work would earn?

items.text: Appraising it against each dimension of the criteria and naming the band it meets and why.
Writing more than other students do.
Submitting the work earlier than required.
Preferring their own work to that of others.

feedback.correct: That's right. Judging each dimension against the criteria is what makes the judgement justifiable.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for how the judgement is tied to the criteria.
feedback.incorrectFinal: A grade can be justified when the work is appraised against each dimension and the band it meets is named. Length, timing or preference do not justify a judgement.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
